title: Upright, not propped up
hookLine: honor the divine spark within you and stand upright, not held upright (Meditations 3.5, 3.12)

lines: A TOMATO PLANT ON A STAKE.
cards: A tomato plant tied to a stake grows tall, but only because something holds it up. Cut the string, and it flops. A young oak in a field has nothing holding it.

It sways in the wind and stays standing. Plenty of people are a bit of both. They lean on praise to feel good, on other people's calm to feel calm, on someone's approval to feel sure they did the right thing.
Marcus noticed that in himself, and wrote a short, blunt sentence about it. Today's word is his name for what holds you up from the inside: daimon.

teach.b: First, the word. Daimon is Greek, and it does not mean demon; that dark meaning came much later.
For Marcus, the daimon is the divine spirit within each person, a fragment, he says elsewhere, of the reason that orders the whole universe, given to each person as a guide. Your inner compass.

The Greek word for happiness, eudaimonia, literally means having a good daimon, and Marcus plays on that himself. In 3.5 he tells himself: let the god within you be the guardian of who you are. Be cheerful.
Don't look for help from outside, or for the calm other people give.
And then, in George Long's translation: "A man then must stand erect, not be kept erect by others." In 3.12 he adds how.
Do the work in front of you seriously and calmly, following reason, keeping your divine part pure, as if you might have to give it back at any moment.
Expect nothing, fear nothing, and be honest in every word. That's the key. A propped-up person has to manage what everyone thinks.
An upright person just has to be true. You don't need to believe in a daimon the way Marcus did to use this. Religious listeners may hear the soul, or conscience, or God's breath in a person.
Others hear integrity. The question is the same: when the string is cut, what holds you up? Marcus's answer is the thing inside that doesn't lie.

how: In the Stoic tradition, the daimon is the guiding reason within each person, and readers of Marcus often use 3.5 and 3.12 as a daily check on honesty and self-reliance.

o: the divine guide within each person
a lucky charm that brings good fortune
an evil spirit that leads people astray

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.

s: for Marcus, daimon means an evil spirit
the demon meaning came much later. for Marcus it's the divine guide within each person.
eudaimonia, happiness, literally means a good daimon
and Marcus plays on the word himself.
Marcus says to rely on the calm other people give you
he tells himself not to seek the calm others give, but to stand upright on his own.

games.q: a friend asks if you liked their plan, and you didn't. what would an upright, not propped, answer be?
o: say you loved it, to be liked.
say honestly, and kindly, what you really think.
games.why: Marcus asks for honesty in every word. being held up from inside means you don't need to manage what everyone thinks.

practice: Sit up tall, spine upright, nothing leaning, and breathe. Think of a moment coming up where you might shade the truth a little to be liked: a compliment you don't mean, a yes that means no, a story you'd polish.
Decide now to say it straight, kindly and plainly.

wordCard.voice: Daimon. Greek for the divine spirit within a person, for Marcus the inner guide to honor; not a demon. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a divine spirit; for Marcus, the guiding god within each person.

carryVoice: Your line: upright, not propped. Held up from the inside, not by anyone's praise. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: A man then must stand erect, not be kept erect by others.
